question: Write the semantic markup for a blog post page, including the document structure, header, main article with title and metadata, and footer.
thoughtProcess: I want sectioning elements that describe the page's regions so assistive tech and search engines understand it. A header for the masthead, a main for the primary content, an article wrapping the post, a header inside the article for its title and metadata, a time element for the publish date with a machine-readable datetime, and a footer for the site. The single h1 is the post title, and section headings inside use h2.

solution.code:
Dev Blog
Articles About

Understanding the Cascade

By Jane Doe · June 20, 2026

The cascade decides which rule wins when several apply.

Specificity

Specificity weighs selectors before source order is used.

Tagged: CSS

© 2026 Dev Blog

lineByLine: The doctype and html with lang=en declare a standards-mode English document. The head sets the charset first, a responsive viewport, and the title. The page header holds the site name and a labelled nav. main wraps the unique page content so assistive tech can jump to it. article is the self-contained post, with its own header carrying the single h1 title and a byline whose time element pairs human text with a machine-readable datetime. A section with an h2 groups a subtopic, and the article's own footer holds post metadata like tags. The page-level footer holds site-wide info.

alternativeApproaches.title: Multiple articles in a feed
alternativeApproaches.explanation: On an index page, wrap each post summary in its own article inside a section or the main, so each is an independently meaningful unit.
alternativeApproaches.code:
Latest articles

Understanding the Cascade

The cascade decides which rule wins...

A Grid Primer

Grid lays out in two dimensions...

alternativeApproaches.title: Div soup (anti-pattern)
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Using div for every region works visually but conveys no structure to assistive tech or crawlers, which is why semantic elements are preferred.

followUps.question: Why use a single h1 per page and h2 for sections?
followUps.answer: A logical heading outline lets screen-reader users navigate by heading and helps search engines understand hierarchy. One h1 names the page or post, and nested headings should not skip levels, so subsections of the article use h2, their subsections h3, and so on.

followUps.question: What does the time element's datetime attribute add?
followUps.answer: It provides a machine-readable timestamp in a standard format alongside the human-friendly text, so browsers, search engines, and tools can parse the exact date even when the visible text is informal like June 20, 2026.

question: Build an accessible primary navigation that marks the current page for assistive technology.
thoughtProcess: Navigation belongs in a nav landmark, and when there are several navs I label each with aria-label so they are distinguishable. The links are real anchors. To indicate which page is active, the most accessible signal is aria-current=page on the active link, which screen readers announce as current. I avoid relying on color alone to show the active state.

solution.code:
• Home
  • Products
  • Pricing
  • Contact

lineByLine: The nav element creates a navigation landmark, and aria-label=Primary names it so a user with multiple navs can tell them apart. An unordered list groups the links, which screen readers announce as a list with an item count, giving structure. Each item is a real anchor with an href so it works without JavaScript and is keyboard focusable. The active link carries aria-current=page, which assistive tech announces as the current page, conveying state independently of any visual styling.

alternativeApproaches.title: aria-current values beyond page
alternativeApproaches.explanation: aria-current also accepts step, location, date, and time for wizards, breadcrumbs, and calendars, plus a generic true, so the right token matches the context.

alternativeApproaches.title: Styling the current link
alternativeApproaches.explanation: You can target the current item visually with the attribute selector so the visual and programmatic state stay in sync.

followUps.question: Why aria-current=page instead of just a CSS active class?
followUps.answer: A CSS class only changes appearance and conveys nothing to a screen reader, so a blind user cannot tell which item is current. aria-current=page exposes the state in the accessibility tree and is announced, while you can still style off the same attribute so visual and programmatic state agree.

followUps.question: When do you need aria-label on a nav?
followUps.answer: When a page has more than one navigation landmark, like a primary nav and a footer nav, each needs a distinct accessible name so users browsing by landmark can tell them apart. With a single nav a label is optional, though it is still good practice.

question: Write the markup for an accessible data table with a caption, column and row headers, and proper scoping.
thoughtProcess: A real data table uses table elements, not divs. I add a caption to give it an accessible name, group the header row in thead and the body in tbody. Each header cell is a th with a scope attribute so screen readers associate data cells with the right headers: scope=col for column headers and scope=row for the first cell of each row that labels the row. This makes the relationships explicit when reading a single cell out of context.

solution.code:
Quarterly revenue by region (USD millions)
Region Q1 Q2
North 12.4 14.1
South 9.8 10.5

lineByLine: The table element marks this as tabular data so assistive tech offers table navigation. The caption gives the table an accessible name read before the contents. thead groups the header row and tbody the data rows, which clarifies structure and aids printing and styling. Each column heading is a th with scope=col, telling screen readers it labels the cells below it. The first cell in each body row is a th with scope=row, labeling that row, so a user landing on the 14.1 cell hears it associated with North and Q2. Plain data cells are td.

alternativeApproaches.title: headers and id for complex tables
alternativeApproaches.explanation: When a table has multiple header levels or spanning headers that scope cannot express, give each header an id and reference them from each cell with the headers attribute for explicit association.

alternativeApproaches.title: tfoot for summary rows
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Totals or summary rows belong in a tfoot, which groups them semantically and lets browsers repeat them when printing long tables.

followUps.question: When should you use the headers/id approach instead of scope?
followUps.answer: scope handles simple tables with one level of row and column headers. For complex tables with multiple header rows, irregular spans, or headers that apply to specific cells in non-obvious ways, the headers attribute referencing header ids gives explicit, unambiguous associations that scope cannot express.

followUps.question: Why not build a table layout with divs and ARIA grid roles?
followUps.answer: Native table elements come with built-in semantics, keyboard table navigation in screen readers, and zero risk of mismatched roles. Recreating that with divs and role=table, row, columnheader, and cell is fragile and easy to get wrong, so you only reach for ARIA grid patterns when you need interactive grid behavior the native table cannot provide.

question: Create a labelled signup form that uses native validation attributes and associates labels, hints, and errors correctly.
thoughtProcess: Every control needs an explicitly associated label via for and id. I use the right input types so mobile keyboards and built-in validation kick in: email, password. Native attributes like required, minlength, type=email, and pattern give validation without JavaScript. I associate help text and error messages with aria-describedby, set autocomplete tokens so password managers and autofill work, and group related controls. A real submit button posts the form.

solution.code:
We'll never share your email.

At least 8 characters.

lineByLine: The form posts to a real endpoint so it works without JavaScript. Each field's label is tied to its input through matching for and id, making the label clickable and giving the input an accessible name. type=email triggers email validation and an email-optimized mobile keyboard, while required marks the field mandatory and minlength enforces a minimum password length, all natively. autocomplete=email and new-password let browsers and password managers fill and suggest correctly. aria-describedby links each input to its hint paragraph so screen readers read the guidance after the label, and the same attribute is where a dynamically inserted error message id would be added. A type=submit button submits the form.

alternativeApproaches.title: Grouping with fieldset and legend
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Related controls, especially radio and checkbox groups, should be wrapped in a fieldset with a legend that names the group for assistive tech.
alternativeApproaches.code:
<fieldset>
  <legend>Notification preference</legend>
  <label><input type="radio" name="notify" value="email" /> Email</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="notify" value="sms" /> SMS</label>
</fieldset>

alternativeApproaches.title: Wrapping label (implicit association)
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Wrapping the input inside the label associates them without for/id, which is convenient but for/id is more robust when markup is generated or rearranged.

followUps.question: How do you expose a validation error message to screen readers?
followUps.answer: Add the error message element's id to the input's aria-describedby so it is announced along with the label, set aria-invalid=true on the field, and put the message in a live region or move focus to it so the user is notified when it appears. Native constraint validation messages are announced automatically, but custom inline errors need this wiring.

followUps.question: Why do autocomplete tokens matter for accessibility and UX?
followUps.answer: Standard autocomplete tokens let browsers and password managers correctly fill fields, which reduces errors and effort for everyone and is especially helpful for users with motor or cognitive disabilities. They also satisfy the WCAG criterion on identifying input purpose, so they are an accessibility requirement, not just a convenience.

question: Write a responsive image using srcset and sizes, and a picture element with art direction and a modern format fallback.
thoughtProcess: There are two distinct needs. For resolution switching, where it is the same image at different sizes, I use img with srcset listing width descriptors and sizes describing the rendered width, letting the browser pick the best file. For art direction, where I want a different crop or a modern format, I use picture with source elements that have media or type conditions and an img fallback. I always include width, height or aspect-ratio and alt text.
lineByLine: In the first example, srcset lists candidate files with width descriptors so the browser knows each file's intrinsic width, and sizes tells it the image renders full width below 600px and half width otherwise, so it can choose the smallest sufficient file for the device's pixel density. width and height reserve space to prevent layout shift, and alt describes the content. In the second example, picture lets the browser pick the first matching source: a portrait crop on narrow screens, otherwise a wide AVIF, then a WebP, each gated by media or type. The img inside is the mandatory fallback for browsers that match no source and the element that actually renders, carrying the alt and dimensions.

alternativeApproaches.title: Pixel-density descriptors
alternativeApproaches.explanation: When an image always renders at a fixed CSS size, use x descriptors instead of w plus sizes to serve higher-resolution files to high-DPI screens.

alternativeApproaches.title: Lazy loading and decoding hints
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Add loading=lazy to defer offscreen images and decoding=async to avoid blocking, improving performance without changing the responsive behavior.

followUps.question: When do you use srcset/sizes versus the picture element?
followUps.answer: Use img with srcset and sizes for resolution switching, where it is the same image and you just want the optimal size for the viewport and density. Use picture when you need art direction, like a different crop per breakpoint, or to offer modern formats with fallbacks via type, because picture gives you explicit, condition-based source selection.

followUps.question: Why are width and height attributes important on responsive images?
followUps.answer: They let the browser compute the image's aspect ratio and reserve the correct space before the file loads, preventing Cumulative Layout Shift. With responsive images the rendered size varies, but the intrinsic width and height still establish the ratio the browser uses to hold the box.

question: Write an accessible figure with an image and a caption.
thoughtProcess: When an image has a caption that describes or comments on it, the figure element groups them and figcaption provides the caption that is programmatically associated with the figure. The alt text and the caption serve different purposes: alt conveys the image content for those who cannot see it, while the caption is supplementary context for everyone. I avoid making them redundant.
lineByLine: The figure element groups the image with its caption as a single self-contained unit that can be referenced and moved without breaking the association. The img has descriptive alt text conveying what the chart shows for users who cannot see it, plus width and height to reserve space. figcaption is the caption, programmatically tied to the figure so assistive tech reads it as belonging to the image, and it offers interpretive context that complements rather than duplicates the alt.

alternativeApproaches.title: figure without an image
alternativeApproaches.explanation: figure is not just for images; it can group a code block, a quotation, or a table with its caption, since it represents any self-contained referenced content.

alternativeApproaches.title: Multiple images in one figure
alternativeApproaches.explanation: A single figure can contain several images sharing one caption, useful for a series or comparison.

followUps.question: How should alt text and figcaption differ?
followUps.answer: alt describes the image's content for people who cannot see it and should stand in for the image, while figcaption is a visible caption providing context, attribution, or commentary for all users. Making them identical is redundant for screen-reader users who would hear the same text twice, so they should complement each other.

followUps.question: Is figcaption required inside figure?
followUps.answer: No, figcaption is optional and there can be at most one, as the first or last child. A figure can stand on its own to mark self-contained content, but when you do include a caption, figcaption is what associates it semantically with the figure's contents.

question: Write a definition list for a set of terms and their descriptions.
thoughtProcess: A definition list is the semantically correct structure for name-value or term-description pairs. dl wraps the list, dt holds each term, and dd holds the description. The structure supports one term with multiple descriptions or multiple terms sharing a description, which is more expressive than a generic list. It is also useful for metadata key-value pairs, not only dictionary definitions.

solution.code:
<dl>
  <dt>HTML</dt>
  <dd>The markup language for structuring web content.</dd>

  <dt>CSS</dt>
  <dd>A language for describing the presentation of markup.</dd>

  <dt>HTTP</dt>
  <dt>HTTPS</dt>
  <dd>Protocols for transferring web resources, the latter encrypted.</dd>
</dl>

lineByLine: The dl element establishes a description list grouping terms with their descriptions. Each dt is a term being defined, and the dd that follows is its description, with assistive tech announcing the association between them. The final group shows two consecutive dt elements sharing a single dd, which the structure supports for terms that share one description, demonstrating that dl expresses relationships a plain ul cannot.

alternativeApproaches.title: Key-value metadata
alternativeApproaches.explanation: dl is appropriate for displaying metadata pairs like product specifications, not only dictionary definitions, because it models term-to-value relationships.

alternativeApproaches.title: Grouping pairs with div
alternativeApproaches.explanation: A div may wrap a dt/dd group inside a dl, which is allowed and helps when styling each pair as a row with flor grid.

followUps.question: When is a dl more appropriate than a ul or a table?
followUps.answer: A dl fits when content is genuinely term-and-description or name-value pairs, like a glossary or metadata, because it encodes that relationship. A ul is for a flat list of similar items with no pairing, and a table is for two-dimensional data with rows and columns; choosing the structure that matches the data's shape keeps the markup meaningful.

followUps.question: Can a single term have multiple descriptions?
followUps.answer: Yes, a dt can be followed by several dd elements when a term has multiple descriptions or values, and conversely multiple consecutive dt elements can share one dd. This flexibility is part of why dl is more expressive than a generic list for paired data.

question: Build an accordion or disclosure widget using native details and summary, with no JavaScript.
thoughtProcess: The details and summary elements provide a native disclosure widget that is keyboard accessible and announces its expanded or collapsed state to screen readers for free. summary is the always-visible label that toggles the rest of the details content. For an accordion of several panels I stack multiple details elements, optionally adding open to the first. This avoids reinventing ARIA expanded state and focus handling.

solution.code:
Frequently asked questions

What is your return policy?

You can return any item within 30 days for a full refund.

Do you ship internationally?

Yes, we ship to most countries; rates are shown at checkout.

How do I track my order?

We email a tracking link as soon as your order ships.

lineByLine: Each details element is a self-contained disclosure that can be opened or closed. Its first child summary is the visible toggle and accessible label; clicking it or pressing Enter or Space toggles the panel, and the browser exposes the expanded state automatically. The content after summary is shown only when the details is open. The open attribute on the first details makes it expanded by default. Stacking several details elements forms an accordion-like FAQ without any JavaScript, with native keyboard support and state announcement.

alternativeApproaches.title: Exclusive accordion with the name attribute
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Giving sibling details elements the same name attribute makes them mutually exclusive, so opening one closes the others, like a traditional accordion, still without scripting.

alternativeApproaches.title: ARIA disclosure pattern with a button
alternativeApproaches.explanation: When you need custom animation or behavior details cannot provide, build it with a button using aria-expanded toggling the controlled panel via aria-controls, implementing the keyboard behavior yourself.

followUps.question: What accessibility does details/summary provide for free?
followUps.answer: It is keyboard operable, focusable, toggles with Enter and Space, and exposes its open or closed state to assistive technology automatically, announcing as an expandable group. Recreating all of that with custom elements and ARIA is error-prone, so the native widget is preferred whenever it meets the need.

followUps.question: How do you make multiple details behave as a single-open accordion?
followUps.answer: Give the related details elements the same name attribute, which groups them so only one can be open at a time, matching classic accordion behavior natively. Before that attribute was supported you needed JavaScript to close siblings, but now it is a pure-markup solution.

question: Write the markup for an accessible modal dialog, including the dialog role, modal semantics, and an accessible name.
thoughtProcess: The native dialog element is the modern choice because showModal gives focus trapping, backdrop, and Escape-to-close for free. I show the markup with the proper semantics either way: role of dialog, aria-modal=true so assistive tech treats background content as inert, and aria-labelledby pointing at the title so the dialog has an accessible name. A close button and a focusable heading round it out. I note the focus-management responsibilities.

solution.code:
Delete project?

This permanently removes the project and all its data.

Session expiring

You will be signed out in 1 minute.

lineByLine: The native dialog element, opened with showModal in script, automatically applies dialog semantics, renders a backdrop, makes background content inert, traps focus, and closes on Escape. aria-labelledby points at the h2 id so the dialog's accessible name is its title, and aria-describedby points at the body text. A form with method=dialog lets the buttons close the dialog and report which one was pressed via their value, and autofocus places initial focus on the primary action. The second block shows the same semantics built manually: role=dialog identifies it, aria-modal=true tells assistive tech the rest of the page is inert, and aria-labelledby supplies the name, though here you must implement focus trapping, Escape handling, and returning focus yourself.

alternativeApproaches.title: Native dialog with the inert attribute
alternativeApproaches.explanation: If supporting a custom modal, mark the rest of the page inert while it is open so background content cannot be focused or read by assistive tech.

alternativeApproaches.title: alertdialog for urgent confirmations
alternativeApproaches.explanation: For interruptive messages requiring a response, role=alertdialog conveys urgency and prompts assistive tech to announce it immediately.

followUps.question: What focus management does an accessible modal require?
followUps.answer: On open, focus must move into the dialog, typically to the first interactive element or the heading; while open, focus must be trapped so Tab cannot reach background content; and on close, focus must return to the element that opened it. The native dialog opened with showModal handles trapping and the backdrop, but you still ensure focus moves in and returns out.

followUps.question: Why prefer the native dialog element over a div with role=dialog?
followUps.answer: The native dialog with showModal provides focus trapping, the top layer, a backdrop, background inertness, and Escape-to-close without custom code, which are exactly the parts people get wrong. A div with role=dialog requires you to implement all of that yourself, so the native element is more robust and less error-prone.

question: Write accessible breadcrumb navigation showing the user's location in the site hierarchy.
thoughtProcess: Breadcrumbs are navigation, so they go in a nav landmark with a descriptive aria-label like Breadcrumb. An ordered list models the hierarchy since order is meaningful. Each level is a link except the current page, which is plain text marked with aria-current=page. I avoid putting separators in the markup as real text, using CSS for the visual chevrons so screen readers do not read them. Optionally I add BreadcrumbList structured data for SEO.

solution.code:
1. Home
  2. Electronics
  3. Phones
  4. Model X Pro

lineByLine: The nav element makes this a navigation landmark, and aria-label=Breadcrumb names it so users can distinguish it from other navs. An ordered list ol is used because the sequence of ancestors is meaningful, from site root to current page, and screen readers announce the position and count. Each ancestor level is a real anchor so users can jump up the hierarchy. The final item is not a link but a span with aria-current=page, signaling to assistive tech that this is the current page and that it is correctly non-navigable. Visual separators between items are added with CSS rather than as text nodes so they are not announced.

alternativeApproaches.title: CSS-generated separators
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Render the chevron or slash with a CSS pseudo-element so it is purely decorative and never read aloud by screen readers.

alternativeApproaches.title: BreadcrumbList structured data
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Adding schema.org BreadcrumbList JSON-LD lets search engines display the breadcrumb trail in results, improving SEO.

followUps.question: Why use an ordered list rather than an unordered one for breadcrumbs?
followUps.answer: Breadcrumbs represent a hierarchy from the site root to the current page where the sequence carries meaning, so an ordered list correctly conveys that the items have a defined order. An unordered list would imply the items are interchangeable, which misrepresents the relationship.

followUps.question: Should the current page in a breadcrumb be a link?
followUps.answer: No, the current page should be plain text marked with aria-current=page rather than a link to itself, since linking to the page you are already on is pointless and can confuse users. Marking it with aria-current also tells assistive tech it is the current location.

question: Embed a video with captions using the track element, plus controls and fallbacks.
thoughtProcess: I use the video element with controls so users get native playback controls. Multiple source elements provide format fallbacks. The key accessibility piece is a track element with kind=captions pointing at a WebVTT file, with srclang and label so users can pick the language; default makes captions show automatically. I add a descriptions track where useful and provide fallback text for browsers that cannot play video. I avoid autoplay with sound.
lineByLine: The video element with controls exposes native play, pause, volume, and caption controls, and poster shows a thumbnail before playback while preload=metadata avoids downloading the whole file upfront. Two source elements offer WebM then MP4 so the browser picks a format it supports. Each track with kind=captions references a WebVTT caption file, with srclang giving the language code and label the human-readable name shown in the caption menu; default tells the browser to enable the English captions initially. The paragraph after the sources is fallback content shown only when the browser cannot render video, offering a download link.

alternativeApproaches.title: Subtitles versus captions
alternativeApproaches.explanation: kind=subtitles is for translating dialogue for users who can hear, while kind=captions also includes non-speech sounds for deaf and hard-of-hearing users; pick the kind that matches the track's purpose.

alternativeApproaches.title: Audio descriptions and chapters
alternativeApproaches.explanation: kind=descriptions provides audio descriptions of visual content, and kind=chapters enables chapter navigation, both improving accessibility and usability.

followUps.question: What is the difference between captions and subtitles in the track element?
followUps.answer: Captions, kind=captions, are intended for users who cannot hear the audio and include dialogue plus relevant non-speech sounds and speaker identification. Subtitles, kind=subtitles, assume the user can hear and mainly translate the spoken dialogue into another language, so they omit sound effects.

followUps.question: Why provide multiple source elements and fallback content?
followUps.answer: Different browsers support different codecs, so offering WebM and MP4 lets each browser choose one it can play. The fallback content inside the video element is shown only to browsers that cannot play any source at all, giving those users a download link rather than a broken element.

question: Write the head block for a product page with title, description, canonical, Open Graph, Twitter card, and Product structured data.
thoughtProcess: The head should carry everything crawlers and social scrapers need, server-rendered. I set charset and viewport first, then a unique title and meta description. A canonical link consolidates duplicate URLs. Open Graph tags drive social previews with an absolute image, and a Twitter card type complements them. Finally a JSON-LD Product block with name, image, offers, price, and availability enables rich results. Values should be unique per product.

solution.code:
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8" />
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1" />

  <title>Aero Running Shoe - Lightweight Trainers | Acme</title>
  <meta
    name="description"
    content="The Aero running shoe weighs just 210g with responsive cushioning. Free shipping and 30-day returns."
  />
  <link rel="canonical" href="https://acme.com/shoes/aero" />

  <meta property="og:type" content="product" />
  <meta property="og:title" content="Aero Running Shoe" />
  <meta property="og:description" content="Lightweight 210g trainers with responsive cushioning." />
  <meta property="og:url" content="https://acme.com/shoes/aero" />
  <meta property="og:image" content="https://acme.com/img/aero-1200x630.jpg" />

  <meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image" />
  <meta name="twitter:title" content="Aero Running Shoe" />
  <meta name="twitter:image" content="https://acme.com/img/aero-1200x630.jpg" />

  <script type="application/ld+json">
  {
    "@context": "https://schema.org",
    "@type": "Product",
    "name": "Aero Running Shoe",
    "image": "https://acme.com/img/aero-1200x630.jpg",
    "description": "Lightweight 210g trainers with responsive cushioning.",
    "offers": {
      "@type": "Offer",
      "priceCurrency": "USD",
      "price": "129.00",
      "availability": "https://schema.org/InStock"
    }
  }
  </script>
</head>

lineByLine: charset and viewport come first so encoding and responsive scaling are set before content. The title is unique and descriptive for the tab and search results, and the meta description gives the snippet text. The canonical link names the authoritative URL to consolidate duplicates. The og: tags supply the social preview: type, title, description, the canonical url, and an absolute image at recommended dimensions. The twitter:card set to summary_large_image opts into a large-image card, falling back to Open Graph for any missing fields. The JSON-LD script declares a schema.org Product with name, image, description, and an Offer carrying currency, price, and availability, which can unlock price-and-availability rich results in search.

alternativeApproaches.title: Adding AggregateRating
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Including review ratings in the Product structured data can surface star ratings in search results when genuine reviews exist.

alternativeApproaches.title: robots meta for indexing control
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Add a robots meta to keep thin or duplicate variants out of the index without blocking crawling.

followUps.question: Why must og:image be an absolute URL at specific dimensions?
followUps.answer: Social scrapers fetch the image independently of the page, so a relative path will not resolve for them, and platforms expect roughly 1200 by 630 for a large card. A correctly sized absolute image ensures the preview renders sharply rather than cropped, blurry, or missing.

followUps.question: How do you keep the JSON-LD price in sync with the displayed price?
followUps.answer: Generate the structured data from the same product data that renders the visible price, so a single source feeds both. Structured data that disagrees with the visible page risks a manual penalty, so binding them to one source and validating with the Rich Results Test prevents drift.

question: Define a reusable Web Component using a custom element, a template, and a slot, registered with an inline script.
thoughtProcess: A Web Component combines a custom element class, a template for its internal markup, and slots so consumers can project their own content. I define a template, then a class extending HTMLElement that attaches a shadow root and clones the template into it in the constructor. The slot lets the light-DOM content the user puts between the tags render inside the shadow DOM. I register it with customElements.define using a hyphenated name. This encapsulates structure and styles.

solution.code: Jane Doe Frontend engineer who loves the platform.

lineByLine: The template element holds inert markup and scoped styles that are not rendered until cloned, so it serves as the component's internal blueprint. Inside it, named slot elements act as placeholders with fallback text shown when no matching content is provided. The user-card usage shows a consumer projecting their own elements into the named slots via the slot attribute. In the script, the UserCard class extends HTMLElement; its constructor calls super, finds the template, attaches an open shadow root, and clones the template content into it, which encapsulates the structure and styles from the rest of the page. customElements.define registers the class under the hyphenated tag name user-card, after which any such element on the page is upgraded to the component.

alternativeApproaches.title: Observed attributes for reactivity
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Declare observedAttributes and implement attributeChangedCallback to react when a consumer changes an attribute, making the component configurable and dynamic.

alternativeApproaches.title: Default (unnamed) slot
alternativeApproaches.explanation: A single unnamed slot projects all of the consumer's child content, useful for wrapper components that do not need named regions.

followUps.question: Why must a custom element name contain a hyphen?
followUps.answer: The hyphen distinguishes custom elements from current and future standard HTML elements, which never contain hyphens, guaranteeing no collision with built-in tags. The parser uses this rule to know an element is a custom element, so customElements.define rejects names without a dash.

followUps.question: What does attaching a shadow root provide?
followUps.answer: It creates an encapsulated subtree where the component's markup and styles are isolated from the surrounding document, so the component's CSS does not leak out and page CSS does not bleed in. Slots then let consumer-provided light DOM content render at defined points inside that shadow tree.

question: Add a skip-to-content link and landmark regions so keyboard and screen-reader users can navigate efficiently.
thoughtProcess: Keyboard users should be able to bypass repetitive navigation, so the first focusable element is a skip link anchored to the main content's id. It is visually hidden until focused so it does not clutter the design but appears for keyboard users. The page uses landmark elements, header, nav, main, aside, footer, so screen-reader users can jump between regions. The main element gets the id the skip link targets and is the single main landmark.

lineByLine: The skip link is the first focusable element in the body, anchored with href=#main to the main content. Its CSS positions it off-screen by default so it stays invisible visually, and the :focus rule brings it on-screen when a keyboard user tabs to it, so they can press Enter to jump past the header and nav straight to the content. The header, nav, main, aside, and footer elements each create a landmark region that screen-reader users can navigate between directly. The main element carries id=main, the skip-link target, and there is exactly one main landmark. The nav and aside have aria-labels so multiple landmarks of the same type stay distinguishable.

alternativeApproaches.title: Clip-based visually-hidden pattern
alternativeApproaches.explanation: A clip-rect or clip-path visually-hidden utility hides the link from sight while keeping it focusable and in the layout flow, an alternative to off-screen positioning.

alternativeApproaches.title: tabindex=-1 on the target
alternativeApproaches.explanation: If focus does not move reliably to the main region on activation, add tabindex=-1 to the target so it can receive programmatic focus after the jump.

followUps.question: Why should the skip link be hidden visually but not with display:none?
followUps.answer: display:none and visibility:hidden remove the element from the tab order and the accessibility tree, so the link would not be focusable at all. The skip link must stay focusable, so it is hidden by positioning it off-screen or clipping it, then revealed on focus for keyboard users.

followUps.question: What do landmark elements give screen-reader users?
followUps.answer: Elements like header, nav, main, aside, and footer expose ARIA landmark roles automatically, letting screen-reader users list and jump directly between major regions of the page. This is faster than reading linearly, and pairing duplicate landmarks with aria-labels keeps them distinguishable.
